thesis: Unreliable generation can aid discovery when independently rejectable evaluation selects results.

ideas.statement: FunSearch demonstrates bounded verified contributions without oracle status.
A hypothesis dossier needs scope, rival, falsifiable test and preserved revision history.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: There is a comfortable way to avoid disappointment: to believe nothing new can be discovered. It is a bad way. It closes the door to research along with the door to illusions.

The right question is not whether an LLM is “allowed” to contribute to a discovery. The question is how we recognize the contribution and what mechanism separates fertile proposals from merely convincing ones. Serious criticism of overconfidence must not become a doctrine of impossibility.

FunSearch, presented by Romera-Paredes and colleagues in Nature, combines program generation with automated evaluation and evolutionary search. The researchers reported new mathematical constructions and improved heuristics for certain problems. Candidate programs were executed and selected by specified evaluators, not accepted for the tone of their explanations. The results are bounded: they do not mean a general solution to all those problems or the complete automation of scientific discovery. [11]

This example should change the discussion. An unreliable generator can participate in a process that produces verifiable results. We need not turn the generator into an oracle. We can change the architecture of the process.

Let us return to Mara. She believes understanding can be described through families of interpretation systems that construct and correct themselves. As a fictional research scenario, the idea cannot be evaluated solely by the beauty of its definition. It must be unpacked.

What does she call an “interpreter”? What inputs does it receive? What change does it produce? How do we distinguish an explanation of understanding from simply renaming it? What task would the architecture solve that a simpler alternative cannot solve at the same cost?

These questions do not reduce philosophy to programming. They separate types of commitment. A philosophical thesis can clarify a concept without immediately producing a benchmark. An engineering claim about reliability must say under what conditions the system is more reliable. A claim about the human mind requires evidence about people, not merely a program that imitates part of their behavior.

We propose giving every important claim a small dossier. Not a sales presentation, but a worksheet containing the statement, its scope of validity, the relevant alternative, the test, and the result that would force us to revise the claim.

For example: “My procedure reduces errors in extracting obligations from documents.” We must specify which documents, what type of error, compared with which method, at what cost, and with what separation between the data used to adjust the method and the data used to evaluate it. If the result appears only on examples used in design, we have a local demonstration, not yet a generalization.

If we change the hypothesis after a negative result, that is allowed and often necessary. But we preserve the history. Otherwise, a hypothesis that made ten wrong predictions can be presented retrospectively as one that anticipated everything.

“Play devil’s advocate” can produce useful objections. But it is not enough. A model can invent weak criticisms and then elegantly defeat them. A real adversary, in the epistemic sense, is something that can reject the result without depending on our wish to continue the story.

It can be an executable test kept separate. It can be a mathematical counterexample. It can be a specialist who receives the claim without an admiring biography of its author. It can be a measurement on new data. Sometimes it is the very user whose problem the product fails to solve.

People are not infallible either. An evaluator can be conservative, inattentive, or self-interested. Independence does not magically produce truth; it reduces certain dependencies and allows challenge. The ideal is not a tribunal beyond criticism, but a procedure in which objections can change the verdict.

Research should not be evaluated by the number of ideas that survived intact. A counterexample can save months of work. A narrower definition can turn a promise that cannot be evaluated into a feasible project. Discovering that two concepts are not equivalent can be the most important result of an exploration.

Mara can end the evening without a private Nobel Prize and with something better: a precise question, a modest hypothesis, a test that can fail, and a clear reason to run it. Hope does not disappear. It becomes capable of learning.
PART III When Conversation Changes Our Relationship with Reality

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Philosophical, engineering and human-mind claims require different evidence; reviewers remain fallible.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
